It is mainly known as “{{ill|Umisachi Yamasa|ja|海幸山幸|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Umisachi Yamasa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 山幸彦と海幸彦|1=Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11468336}}” (うみさちやまさち). == Overview == Within the myth, the naming as recorded in the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]] is as follows: ;Kojiki Nomenclature :'''Yamasachihiko''' – [[:en:Hoori|Hikohodemi]] (in the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]]) and Hikohodemi (in the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]]) :'''Umisachihiko''' – [[:en:Hoderi|Hoteri]] (in the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]]) and KouRankou (in the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]]) As their names imply, the tale tells of the younger Yamasachihiko, skilled in mountain hunting ([[:en:Mountain|Mountain]]), and the elder Umisachihiko, adept at fishing in the sea ([[:en:Sea|Sea]]). The [[:en:Brother|Brothers]] at one time exchanged their implements: Yamasachihiko went fishing ([[:en:Angling|Fishing for Fish]]) but lost the borrowed {{ill|Fishing Hook|ja|釣針|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fishing Hook|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 釣り針|1=fishing hook|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q205276}}, while his elder brother could not procure his game with his own tools. In his distress, Yamasachihiko was instructed by {{ill|Shiotsuchi-no-Oji|lt=Shiotsuchi-no-Oji|lt=Shiotsuchi no Oji|ja|シオツチオジ|lt=Shiochitsu no Kami|lt_ja=塩椎神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shiotsuchi no Oji|qq=}} (also read “しおつちのかみ”) to board a small boat and head for the {{ill|Watatsumi Shrine|ja|綿津見神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Watatsumi Shrine|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (also understood as the Palace of the Sea God). Welcomed by the sea deity ([[:en:Watatsumi|Great Watatsumi]]), Yamasachihiko later married the daughter [[:en:Toyotama-hime|Toyotamahime]] (also known as Toyotamahime, i.e. {{ill|Toyotamahime|ja|豊玉毘売命|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyotamahime|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to トヨタマヒメ|1=Toyotama-hime|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2329261}}) and enjoyed three blissful years at the Watatsumi Shrine. However, needing to return to the land, Yamasachihiko received from Toyotamahime the lost fishing hook along with two mystically endowed orbs, “Shioyutsutama” (潮盈珠) and “Shiohifurutama” (潮乾珠). Using these, he is said to have subdued Umisachihiko and compelled him to pledge loyalty. This Umisachihiko is also regarded as the progenitor of the trading [[:en:Hayato people|Hayato]] tribe. Subsequently, Toyotamahime bore a child – identified as [[:en:Ugayafukiaezu|Ugayafukiaezu]] (reading: うがやふきあえずのみこと) – and Yamasachihiko came to be recognized as the grandfather of [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]] (via his link to the [[:en:Grandparent|Grandfather]]). == Synopsis == === Kojiki === ==== Umisachibiko and Yamasachibiko ==== In the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]], {{ill|Hoteri|ja|火照命|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hoteri|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ホデリ|1=Hoderi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2716491}} (ほでりのみこと) is portrayed as Umisachibiko, a fisherman who caught fish of all sizes, while {{ill|Hikohodemi|ja|火遠理命|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hikohodemi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ホオリ|1=Hoori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1051960}} (ほおりのみこと) is depicted as Yamasachibiko, a hunter who captured beasts of every size. Hikohodemi proposed that the brothers exchange their tools; though Hoteri refused thrice, he eventually consented to a temporary swap. Using his brother’s fishing hook (referred to as “Umisachi”), Hikohodemi attempted to catch fish but failed utterly—and, to make matters worse, lost the hook in the sea. When Hoteri, unable to secure any catch with his own implements, demanded the return of his original tool with the remark, “Neither mountain nor sea yield their fortunes unless one uses one’s own implements,” he reproached his brother. In despair, Hikohodemi fashioned 1,000 hooks from his own {{ill|Ten Fist Sword|ja|十拳剣|1=Totsuka-no-Tsurugi|lt=Ten Fist Sword (alternate)|lt_ja=十拳劔|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ten Fist Sword|13=User:Immanuelle/Totsuka-no-Tsurugi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 十束剣}}, yet Hoteri insisted he desired only the original. ==== Watatsumi God's Palace ==== Hikohodemi then set out for the palace of the sea deity at the {{ill|Watatsumi Shrine|ja|綿津見神の宮殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Watatsumi Shrine|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (originally linked via the anchor in the “Ryūgū” article). While waiting there, a [[:en:Handmaiden|maidservant]] of the sea god’s daughter, [[:en:Toyotama-hime|Toyotamahime]], went out to draw water. When Hikohodemi requested water, the maidservant filled a vessel and presented it; however, instead of drinking, he placed an orb he wore about his neck into the vessel. The orb clung stubbornly to the vessel, prompting the maidservant to relay the incident to Toyotamahime. Startled by the sight of Hikohodemi, Toyotamahime fell in love at first sight. Her father, the sea god himself, emerged and declared that Hikohodemi was none other than the son of {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi|ja|邇々芸命|lt=Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi|lt_ja=邇々芸命|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninigi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (a descendant of the heavenly grandson revered by the fish for their pledged loyalty), and immediately arranged for their marriage. Thus, Hikohodemi lived for three years in the palace of the sea god. ==== Submission of Hoteri ==== After three years, recalling his original purpose for having come, Hoteri lamented deeply. When the sea god inquired about the cause of his sorrow, Hoteri explained. Gathering the fish, the sea god discovered that one red [[:en:Red seabream|Red Sea Bream]] had the lost hook snagged in its throat. He then presented Hoteri with the fishing hook along with the orbs “Shioyutsutama” and “Shiohifurutama,” instructing him: “Return this hook to your brother while uttering: ‘This hook, be it a hook of melancholy, disquiet, poverty, or foolishness,’ and then, if your brother builds a rice field on high ground, you must build yours on low ground; if he builds on low, you build on high. Should he attack, submerge him with Shioyutsutama; and if, in suffering, he begs forgiveness, rescue him with Shiohifurutama.” He then sent him off riding on {{ill|Wani (mythology)|ja|和邇 (神話)|lt=Wani|lt_ja=和邇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wani (mythology)|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 和邇|1=wani|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q20049265}}, now identified as {{ill|Saimotonomi|ja|佐比持神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saimotonomi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. Hoteri thus returned the hook as directed and cultivated his own fields accordingly. As the sea god controlled the waters, Hoteri’s fields were left parched, and he grew increasingly impoverished. Moreover, when Hoteri became wrathful and launched an attack, Hoteri used Shioyutsutama to submerge him; and when Hoteri, wracked with pain, repented, Shiohifurutama was used to rescue him. Repeating this cycle until his torment abated, Hoteri finally bowed his head and vowed to guard Hoteri day and night. ==== The Birth of Toyotamahime ==== After conceiving at the sea palace, Toyotamahime could not bear to deliver a child in the depths and ascended to the land. Intending to build a delivery hut by the seashore, she went into labor before the thatched roof (made of egret feathers) could be completed, and thus entered the delivery hut. She instructed Hikohodemi, “When a person of another land gives birth, they assume their true form. I too intend to deliver in my true form, so under no circumstances should you look inside.” However, curious, Hikohodemi peered inside the hut and witnessed Toyotamahime transformed into Yahiro Wani, with her belly undulating like a serpent. Horrified, he fled. Ashamed of having spied, Toyotamahime, in her distress, returned to the sea, leaving behind the newborn child, who came to be known as [[:en:Ugayafukiaezu|Amatsu Hikohiko Nagakate Ukayafukiaezu]]. Nonetheless, harboring resentment over his peering, Hoteri, in order to raise the child, sent his younger sister [[:en:Tamayori-hime (mother of Jimmu)|Toyotamahime]] along with a parting song exchanged between them. === Nihon Shoki, Section 10 === In the main text of volume 2 of the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]], it is said that the elder, Hoteri, naturally possessed a fishing hook (representing “Umisachi”), while the younger, Hikohodemi, naturally possessed a bow and arrow (representing “Yamasachi”). Initially, the two brothers conversed and decided to test their fortunes by an exchange; but neither managed to obtain any catch. The elder, in his remorse, returned his brother’s bow and demanded his own hook. The younger, having already lost the hook in the sea and unable to retrieve it, fashioned another from his side-sword, assembling a heap in a single basket, but his brother rejected it, insisting instead on the original hook. In despair, Hikohodemi wandered along the seashore, lamenting. There he encountered {{ill|Salt-and-Earth Old Man|ja|塩土老翁|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Salt-and-Earth Old Man|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to シオツチオジ|1=Shiotsuchi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11174872}}, who said, “Worry not; I shall devise a plan for you.” The old man constructed a basket and placed Hikohodemi inside before setting him adrift at sea. In time, he reached a fine shore; abandoning the basket, he proceeded and soon arrived at the sea god’s palace. There, the palace was arranged with the elegance of a princely abode. By a well at the gate grew a tree of {{ill|Yutsukatsura|ja|湯津杜|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yutsukatsura|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, its branches and leaves spreading wide. As Hikohodemi advanced beneath the tree in a state of aimless wandering, a beautiful maiden opened a door and stepped out to fetch water using a lovely bowl. When she saw him, she stared intently; startled, she hurried back and informed her parents, “There is a most rare guest beneath the tree by the well at the gate.” The sea god then spread out multiple layers of tatami mats to welcome him, seating him with courtesy and inquiring the reason for his arrival. Hikohodemi explained his circumstances. When the sea god gathered fish to question them, all answered, “We know not—only that a red-finned fish with a troubled mouth (possibly a red [[:en:Red seabream|Red Sea Bream]]) has appeared.” Upon inspecting the fish’s mouth, the lost hook was recovered. Thereafter, Hikohodemi married the sea god’s daughter, Toyotamahime, and dwelled in the sea palace for three years. Although life there was peaceful and joyful, his longing for his homeland would sometimes bring deep sighs. Hearing this, Toyotamahime said to her father, “Surely the heavenly grandson laments, for he must miss his native land.” The sea god then summoned Hikohodemi, presented him with the previously retrieved hook, and instructed: “When you return this hook to your brother, quietly call it ‘the hook of poverty, of misfortune, of despair, and of folly.’” He also bestowed upon him the orbs “Shioyutsutama” and “Shiohifurutama,” advising: “Dip the former and your brother will be overwhelmed by the tide; if he repents, dip the latter and he shall be restored. In this way, he will naturally submit.” When it came time to depart, Toyotamahime told the heavenly grandson, “I am with child; the time for delivery is near. Please, construct a delivery room for me by the seashore.” Hikohodemi then returned to his original palace and followed the sea god’s instructions. Meanwhile, Hoteri, beset by troubles, eventually submitted, proclaiming, “From now on, I shall be your servant. Please show me mercy.” Thus, in accordance with his request, he was spared—and Hoteri is said to be the ancestor of figures such as Atano-kimi and small bridge figures, among others. Later, as promised, Toyotamahime, accompanied by her younger sister {{ill|Toyotamahime|ja|玉依姫|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyotamahime|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タマヨリビメ|1=Tamayori-hime|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q56344982}}, arrived at the seashore defying the wind and waves. As delivery neared, she entreated, “When I give birth, do not gaze into the delivery room.” Unable to contain his curiosity, the heavenly grandson secretly peered in. Transforming into a dragon, Toyotamahime, deeply ashamed of being spied upon, wrapped her newborn child in straw and abandoned it by the shore, then swiftly departed by sealing off the seacoast. The child came to be known as {{ill|Amatsu Hikohiko Nagakate Ukayafukiaezu|ja|彦波瀲武盧茲草葺不合尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amatsu Hikohiko Nagakate Ukayafukiaezu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. Some time later, Hikohodemi passed away, and it is said he was interred on a tumulus atop Takaya-yama in Himuka. ==== First Account (1) ==== The elder, {{ill|Hanoseri|ja|ホスセリ|lt=Hanoseri|lt_ja=火酢芹命|1=Hosuseri|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanoseri|13=User:Immanuelle/Hosuseri|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 火須勢理命}}, frequently obtained fortune from the sea, while the younger, Hikohodemi, often procured fortune from the mountains. At one time, the brothers agreed to exchange their fortunes. The elder ventured into the mountains with his brother’s bow but could not even find a trace of animal tracks; the younger, taking his brother’s fishing hook, went to the sea but caught no fish and lost the hook. When the elder returned the bow and demanded his original hook, the younger, in anguish, crafted a multitude of hooks from his side-sword and presented them in a basket, yet his brother angrily refused them, insisting on the original. Overwhelmed with sorrow, Hikohodemi wandered by the seashore until an old man appeared, calling himself Salt-and-Earth Old Man, and asked, “Who are you, and why do you suffer here?” After Hikohodemi explained, the old man took a black comb from his bag, tossed it onto the ground, and it transformed into a grove of 500 bamboo shoots. Gathering the bamboo, he constructed a large basket, placed Hikohodemi inside, and set him adrift into the sea. Alternatively, he fashioned a floating vessel from a bamboo basket and thin ropes, binding Hikohodemi to it before sending him off. Eventually, at the bottom of the sea a fine shore appeared naturally, and upon proceeding along it, Hikohodemi soon reached the palace of the sea god. There, the palace was as a castle—lofty and resplendent. Near a well outside the gate, beneath a Katsura tree, a beautiful maiden emerged from among her attendants to fetch water in a jewel-like vessel. Startled, she hurried back and told her divine parents, “There is a rare and noble guest beneath the tree by the well—truly of an uncommon appearance.” ==== First Account (2) ==== Hikohodemi, in his despair, wandered along a hundred-branch grove by a well; then an elderly man appeared, identified as Salt-and-Earth Old Man, and said, “Who are you, and why do you suffer?” After hearing his story, the old man produced a dark comb, threw it to the ground where it transformed into a grove of 500 bamboos, fashioned a large basket, and enclosed Hikohodemi within it before setting him adrift into the sea. (Or, alternatively, he made a floating vessel from a bamboo basket, bound him with thin ropes, and sent him off.) As the tide receded along the shore, the lost hook was recovered from the mouth of a fish, and the sea god called for it. He then returned the hook to Hikohodemi with instructions: when you return this hook to your brother, recite an incantation naming it “the root of poverty, the beginning of famine, the source of suffering.” Moreover, when you cross the sea, I will surely raise a tempest so that you shall not drown.[http://nihon.syoukoukai.com/modules/stories/index.php?lid=1470]{{ill|Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko|ja|海彦と山彦|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 山幸彦と海幸彦|1=Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11468336}} (Manga Japanese Folktales Database) ==== First Account (3) ==== The elder, {{ill|Hanoseri|ja|ホスセリ|lt=Hanoseri|lt_ja=火酢芹命|1=Hosuseri|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanoseri|13=User:Immanuelle/Hosuseri|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 火須勢理命}}, having acquired much from the sea, came to be called Umisachihiko, while the younger, Hikohodemi, who gained much from the mountains, was called Yamasachihiko. Although the elder repeatedly lost his tools to wind and rain, the younger never did. One day, the elder proposed an exchange of fortunes with his brother; the elder took the younger’s bow, venturing into the mountains to hunt, while the younger took the elder’s fishing hook to fish in the sea—yet neither secured any catch and returned empty-handed. When the elder, having reclaimed the bow, demanded his original hook, the younger, at a loss, fashioned a new hook from his side-sword and presented it en masse in a basket. Enraged, the elder declared, “I still desire my original hook!” In his despair, Hikohodemi could only lament. Later, while wandering and sighing bitterly by the sea, he encountered an elderly man who identified himself as Salt-and-Earth Old Man. After hearing his tale, the old man produced a mysterious object from a bag and, casting it to the ground, transformed it into a grove of bamboo. He then constructed a basket and placed Hikohodemi inside, setting him adrift. In time, Hikohodemi reached the palace of the sea god, where the deity, recognizing the divine virtue in the younger, eventually relented and made him his servant. It is said that the descendants of {{ill|Hanoseri|ja|ホスセリ|lt=Hanoseri|lt_ja=火酢芹命|1=Hosuseri|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanoseri|13=User:Immanuelle/Hosuseri|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 火須勢理命}}, the forebears of the Hayato, still remain near the palace walls as ever-vigilant watchdogs.{{Cite book |language=ja |title=隼人（古代の南部九州の居住民） |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E9%9A%BC%E4%BA%BA%28%E5%8F%A4%E4%BB%A3%E3%81%AE%E5%8D%97%E9%83%A8%E4%B9%9D%E5%B7%9E%E3%81%AE%E5%B1%85%E4%BD%8F%E6%B0%91%29-1578344 |publisher=[[:en:Kotobank|Kotobank]] |author1=Shōgakukan Nihon Daihyakusen (Nipponica) |authorlink1=小学館 }} ==== First Account (4) ==== Here, Hikohodemi came to be known as {{ill|Hoiorisuru|ja|火折尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hoiorisuru|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ホオリ|1=Hoori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1051960}} until he encountered Salt-and-Earth Old Man; the narrative from Account (3) is similar. The old man then said, “Fret not; I shall now contrive a plan.” Measuring and declaring, “The excellent steed upon which the sea god rides is none other than an 1‐sun (approximately 30 cm) sea crocodile. Its back is erected at Tachibana’s small gate—indeed, let us devise a scheme with it.” Accompanied by Hoiorisuru, they set out to inspect. At that time, a sea crocodile announced, “After eight days, I shall deliver the heavenly grandson to the sea palace. However, my noble steed is but a 1‐sun crocodile. In a single day, it will surely be accomplished. Now, I must return to summon my lord; ride well and enter the sea. When you do so, a fine shore will naturally appear along the course, and if you proceed along it, you will undoubtedly reach my lord’s palace. At the palace gate, above the well, a Yutsukatsura tree shall be found—take your place there.” No sooner had he spoken than he plunged into the sea. Accordingly, the heavenly grandson waited as instructed; when eight days had passed, a 1‐sun sea crocodile arrived, and he boarded it to enter the sea—each act in accordance with the crocodile’s earlier counsel. Meanwhile, as Toyotamahime’s attendant, bearing a jewel-like bowl, attempted to draw water from the well and noticed a figure at the bottom, she could not manage to scoop the water and looked up at the heavenly grandson. Immediately, she returned to report to her lord, “Our lord appears uniquely resplendent—indeed, a solitary guest of surpassing excellence is present; he is far superior.” The sea god, upon hearing this, said, “I shall observe this.” He then prepared three mats and received the guest. There, the heavenly grandson sat with his feet on the edge of the mat, his hands pressed on the inner mat, and on a sumptuous futon he reclined. Recognizing him as the heavenly god’s grandson, the sea god’s veneration grew ever deeper. Later, when the sea god summoned the red-finned maiden ({{ill|Red Sea Bream|ja|赤鯛|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Red Sea Bream|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}/{{ill|Nayoshi|ja|鯔魚・なよし|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nayoshi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) and inquired, she produced the fishing hook from her mouth. At that moment, the sea god imparted it to Hikohodemi with the command: “When you return this hook to your brother, speak these words: ‘O great hook, the hook of poverty, of destitution, and of idiocy,’ and then, after finishing your speech, cast it aside.” He further instructed that when your brother ventures into the sea to fish, you should remain by the shore to raise a wind—namely, a gust that is a whistle. Thus, I will raise the western and border winds to send forth surging waves to overwhelm him.” Hoiorisuru then returned, having faithfully followed the sea god’s instructions. On the day the elder fished, the younger whistled by the shore; in an instant, a swift wind arose, and the elder, overwhelmed, began to drown with no hope of rescue. In desperation, he called out to his distant brother, “You have long tarried on the open sea; surely there must be a way—please, save me! If I survive, may I forever remain as your servant, or even be known as a ‘dog-man.’ I implore you.” Hearing this, the younger ceased his whistling, and the wind died away. The elder, realizing the divine virtue possessed by his brother, finally submitted. Thus, when the younger produced Shioyutsutama, the elder raised his hands and was engulfed by the tide; when Shiohifurutama was presented, he was restored. Prior to this, as they were parting, Toyotamahime had said, “I am already with child; very soon I shall deliver. Please build a delivery hut for me by the seashore.” Following her words, Toyotamahime later arrived and said to Hikohodemi, “Tonight, I intend to give birth. Do not come near.” Hikohodemi, however, disobeyed and lit a fire on a comb to peep in. In response, Toyotamahime transformed into a massive eight-span crocodile and crawled prostrate. Deeply shamed, she vowed never again to suffer such humiliation and, after wrapping her child in straw and placing it by the shore, departed into the sea. Alternatively, it is said that rather than abandoning her child on the shore, Toyotamahime herself carried the infant and left, later declaring that “It is not proper for the heavenly grandson’s child to be left in the sea,” and thus she entrusted her child to her younger sister, {{ill|Toyotamahime|ja|玉依姫|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyotamahime|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タマヨリビメ|1=Tamayori-hime|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q56344982}}. Soon after, disturbed by the child’s handsome appearance, Toyotamahime’s compassion grew, and she wished to reclaim the child for rearing; but being unable to do so on principle, she sent her younger sister to care for him, along with a parting song. == Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko == The “Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko” myth has exerted a great influence on Japanese folktales and is transmitted throughout Japan in the form of “{{ill|Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko|ja|海彦と山彦|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 山幸彦と海幸彦|1=Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11468336}}.” == Influence on the Urashima Tarō Legend == This myth of “Umisachihiko and Yamasachihiko” is said to have served as a model for the various local legends of [[:en:Urashima Tarō|Urashima Tarō]] throughout Japan.[https://www.asukanet.gr.jp/tobira/urashima/urashima.html][[:en:Urashima Tarō|Urashima Tarō]] (Ancient History [[:en:Hoori|Hoori]]（{{ill|Hikohohodemi|ja|ヒコホホデミ|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hikohohodemi|1=Hikohohodemi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11329989}}）。]] '''Yamasachihiko to Umisachihiko''' (山幸彦と海幸彦) is, in the {{ill|Kiki|ja|記紀|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Kiki|WD=Q842308}}, a mythologized struggle between the {{ill|Tenson-zoku|fr|ja|天孫族|zh|天孫民族|en:draft|simple|User:Immanuelle/Tenson-zoku|ko|천손족|uk|Тенсон Зоку|lt=Tenson Tribe|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenson-zoku|qq=}} and the [[:en:Hayato people|Hayato Tribe]].[http://dictionary.goo.ne.jp/leaf/jn2/20434/m0u/]{{ill|Digital Daijisen|ja|デジタル大辞泉|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Digital Daijisen|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大辞泉|1=Daijisen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q5209153}} [[:en:Shogakukan|Shōgakukan]]（{{ill|Umisachi Yamasa|ja|海幸山幸|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Umisachi Yamasa|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 山幸彦と海幸彦|1=Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11468336}}） 2013-09-11 viewed{{Cite book |language=ja |title={{ill|Umisachi Yamasa|ja|海幸山幸|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Umisachi Yamasa|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 山幸彦と海幸彦|1=Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11468336}} |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%B5%B7%E5%B9%B8%E5%B1%B1%E5%B9%B8-441493#E5.A4.A7.E8.BE.9E.E6.9E.97.20.E7.AC.AC.E4.B8.89.E7.89.88 |publisher=[[:en:Kotobank|Kotobank]] |author1=Sanseidō Daijirin Third Edition |authorlink1=大辞林 }} . It is mainly known as “{{ill|Umisachi Yamasa|ja|海幸山幸|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Umisachi Yamasa|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 山幸彦と海幸彦|1=Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11468336}}” (うみさちやまさち). == Overview == Within the myth, the naming as recorded in the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]] is as follows: ;Kojiki Nomenclature :'''Yamasachihiko''' – [[:en:Hoori|Hikohodemi]] (in the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]]) and Hikohodemi (in the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]]) :'''Umisachihiko''' – [[:en:Hoderi|Hoteri]] (in the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]]) and KouRankou (in the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]]) As their names imply, the tale tells of the younger Yamasachihiko, skilled in mountain hunting ([[:en:Mountain|Mountain]]), and the elder Umisachihiko, adept at fishing in the sea ([[:en:Sea|Sea]]). The [[:en:Brother|Brothers]] at one time exchanged their implements: Yamasachihiko went fishing ([[:en:Angling|Fishing for Fish]]) but lost the borrowed {{ill|Fishing Hook|ja|釣針|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fishing Hook|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 釣り針|1=fishing hook|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q205276}}, while his elder brother could not procure his game with his own tools. In his distress, Yamasachihiko was instructed by {{ill|Shiotsuchi-no-Oji|lt=Shiotsuchi-no-Oji|lt=Shiotsuchi no Oji|ja|シオツチオジ|lt=Shiochitsu no Kami|lt_ja=塩椎神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shiotsuchi no Oji|qq=}} (also read “しおつちのかみ”) to board a small boat and head for the {{ill|Watatsumi Shrine|ja|綿津見神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Watatsumi Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (also understood as the Palace of the Sea God). Welcomed by the sea deity ([[:en:Watatsumi|Great Watatsumi]]), Yamasachihiko later married the daughter [[:en:Toyotama-hime|Toyotamahime]] (also known as Toyotamahime, i.e. {{ill|Toyotamahime|ja|豊玉毘売命|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyotamahime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to トヨタマヒメ|1=Toyotama-hime|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2329261}}) and enjoyed three blissful years at the Watatsumi Shrine. However, needing to return to the land, Yamasachihiko received from Toyotamahime the lost fishing hook along with two mystically endowed orbs, “Shioyutsutama” (潮盈珠) and “Shiohifurutama” (潮乾珠). Using these, he is said to have subdued Umisachihiko and compelled him to pledge loyalty. This Umisachihiko is also regarded as the progenitor of the trading [[:en:Hayato people|Hayato]] tribe. Subsequently, Toyotamahime bore a child – identified as [[:en:Ugayafukiaezu|Ugayafukiaezu]] (reading: うがやふきあえずのみこと) – and Yamasachihiko came to be recognized as the grandfather of [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]] (via his link to the [[:en:Grandparent|Grandfather]]). == Synopsis == === Kojiki === ==== Umisachibiko and Yamasachibiko ==== In the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]], {{ill|Hoteri|ja|火照命|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hoteri|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ホデリ|1=Hoderi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2716491}} (ほでりのみこと) is portrayed as Umisachibiko, a fisherman who caught fish of all sizes, while {{ill|Hikohodemi|ja|火遠理命|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hikohodemi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ホオリ|1=Hoori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1051960}} (ほおりのみこと) is depicted as Yamasachibiko, a hunter who captured beasts of every size. Hikohodemi proposed that the brothers exchange their tools; though Hoteri refused thrice, he eventually consented to a temporary swap. Using his brother’s fishing hook (referred to as “Umisachi”), Hikohodemi attempted to catch fish but failed utterly—and, to make matters worse, lost the hook in the sea. When Hoteri, unable to secure any catch with his own implements, demanded the return of his original tool with the remark, “Neither mountain nor sea yield their fortunes unless one uses one’s own implements,” he reproached his brother. In despair, Hikohodemi fashioned 1,000 hooks from his own {{ill|Ten Fist Sword|ja|十拳剣|1=Totsuka-no-Tsurugi|lt=Ten Fist Sword (alternate)|lt_ja=十拳劔|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ten Fist Sword|13=User:Immanuelle/Totsuka-no-Tsurugi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 十束剣}}, yet Hoteri insisted he desired only the original. ==== Watatsumi God's Palace ==== Hikohodemi then set out for the palace of the sea deity at the {{ill|Watatsumi Shrine|ja|綿津見神の宮殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Watatsumi Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (originally linked via the anchor in the “Ryūgū” article). While waiting there, a [[:en:Handmaiden|maidservant]] of the sea god’s daughter, [[:en:Toyotama-hime|Toyotamahime]], went out to draw water. When Hikohodemi requested water, the maidservant filled a vessel and presented it; however, instead of drinking, he placed an orb he wore about his neck into the vessel. The orb clung stubbornly to the vessel, prompting the maidservant to relay the incident to Toyotamahime. Startled by the sight of Hikohodemi, Toyotamahime fell in love at first sight. Her father, the sea god himself, emerged and declared that Hikohodemi was none other than the son of {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi|ja|邇々芸命|lt=Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi|lt_ja=邇々芸命|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninigi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (a descendant of the heavenly grandson revered by the fish for their pledged loyalty), and immediately arranged for their marriage. Thus, Hikohodemi lived for three years in the palace of the sea god. ==== Submission of Hoteri ==== After three years, recalling his original purpose for having come, Hoteri lamented deeply. When the sea god inquired about the cause of his sorrow, Hoteri explained. Gathering the fish, the sea god discovered that one red [[:en:Red seabream|Red Sea Bream]] had the lost hook snagged in its throat. He then presented Hoteri with the fishing hook along with the orbs “Shioyutsutama” and “Shiohifurutama,” instructing him: “Return this hook to your brother while uttering: ‘This hook, be it a hook of melancholy, disquiet, poverty, or foolishness,’ and then, if your brother builds a rice field on high ground, you must build yours on low ground; if he builds on low, you build on high. Should he attack, submerge him with Shioyutsutama; and if, in suffering, he begs forgiveness, rescue him with Shiohifurutama.” He then sent him off riding on {{ill|Wani (mythology)|ja|和邇 (神話)|lt=Wani|lt_ja=和邇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wani (mythology)|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 和邇|1=wani|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q20049265}}, now identified as {{ill|Saimotonomi|ja|佐比持神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saimotonomi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. Hoteri thus returned the hook as directed and cultivated his own fields accordingly. As the sea god controlled the waters, Hoteri’s fields were left parched, and he grew increasingly impoverished. Moreover, when Hoteri became wrathful and launched an attack, Hoteri used Shioyutsutama to submerge him; and when Hoteri, wracked with pain, repented, Shiohifurutama was used to rescue him. Repeating this cycle until his torment abated, Hoteri finally bowed his head and vowed to guard Hoteri day and night. ==== The Birth of Toyotamahime ==== After conceiving at the sea palace, Toyotamahime could not bear to deliver a child in the depths and ascended to the land. Intending to build a delivery hut by the seashore, she went into labor before the thatched roof (made of egret feathers) could be completed, and thus entered the delivery hut. She instructed Hikohodemi, “When a person of another land gives birth, they assume their true form. I too intend to deliver in my true form, so under no circumstances should you look inside.” However, curious, Hikohodemi peered inside the hut and witnessed Toyotamahime transformed into Yahiro Wani, with her belly undulating like a serpent. Horrified, he fled. Ashamed of having spied, Toyotamahime, in her distress, returned to the sea, leaving behind the newborn child, who came to be known as [[:en:Ugayafukiaezu|Amatsu Hikohiko Nagakate Ukayafukiaezu]]. Nonetheless, harboring resentment over his peering, Hoteri, in order to raise the child, sent his younger sister [[:en:Tamayori-hime (mother of Jimmu)|Toyotamahime]] along with a parting song exchanged between them. === Nihon Shoki, Section 10 === In the main text of volume 2 of the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]], it is said that the elder, Hoteri, naturally possessed a fishing hook (representing “Umisachi”), while the younger, Hikohodemi, naturally possessed a bow and arrow (representing “Yamasachi”). Initially, the two brothers conversed and decided to test their fortunes by an exchange; but neither managed to obtain any catch. The elder, in his remorse, returned his brother’s bow and demanded his own hook. The younger, having already lost the hook in the sea and unable to retrieve it, fashioned another from his side-sword, assembling a heap in a single basket, but his brother rejected it, insisting instead on the original hook. In despair, Hikohodemi wandered along the seashore, lamenting. There he encountered {{ill|Salt-and-Earth Old Man|ja|塩土老翁|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Salt-and-Earth Old Man|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to シオツチオジ|1=Shiotsuchi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11174872}}, who said, “Worry not; I shall devise a plan for you.” The old man constructed a basket and placed Hikohodemi inside before setting him adrift at sea. In time, he reached a fine shore; abandoning the basket, he proceeded and soon arrived at the sea god’s palace. There, the palace was arranged with the elegance of a princely abode. By a well at the gate grew a tree of {{ill|Yutsukatsura|ja|湯津杜|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yutsukatsura|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, its branches and leaves spreading wide. As Hikohodemi advanced beneath the tree in a state of aimless wandering, a beautiful maiden opened a door and stepped out to fetch water using a lovely bowl. When she saw him, she stared intently; startled, she hurried back and informed her parents, “There is a most rare guest beneath the tree by the well at the gate.” The sea god then spread out multiple layers of tatami mats to welcome him, seating him with courtesy and inquiring the reason for his arrival. Hikohodemi explained his circumstances. When the sea god gathered fish to question them, all answered, “We know not—only that a red-finned fish with a troubled mouth (possibly a red [[:en:Red seabream|Red Sea Bream]]) has appeared.” Upon inspecting the fish’s mouth, the lost hook was recovered. Thereafter, Hikohodemi married the sea god’s daughter, Toyotamahime, and dwelled in the sea palace for three years. Although life there was peaceful and joyful, his longing for his homeland would sometimes bring deep sighs. Hearing this, Toyotamahime said to her father, “Surely the heavenly grandson laments, for he must miss his native land.” The sea god then summoned Hikohodemi, presented him with the previously retrieved hook, and instructed: “When you return this hook to your brother, quietly call it ‘the hook of poverty, of misfortune, of despair, and of folly.’” He also bestowed upon him the orbs “Shioyutsutama” and “Shiohifurutama,” advising: “Dip the former and your brother will be overwhelmed by the tide; if he repents, dip the latter and he shall be restored. In this way, he will naturally submit.” When it came time to depart, Toyotamahime told the heavenly grandson, “I am with child; the time for delivery is near. Please, construct a delivery room for me by the seashore.” Hikohodemi then returned to his original palace and followed the sea god’s instructions. Meanwhile, Hoteri, beset by troubles, eventually submitted, proclaiming, “From now on, I shall be your servant. Please show me mercy.” Thus, in accordance with his request, he was spared—and Hoteri is said to be the ancestor of figures such as Atano-kimi and small bridge figures, among others. Later, as promised, Toyotamahime, accompanied by her younger sister {{ill|Toyotamahime|ja|玉依姫|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyotamahime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タマヨリビメ|1=Tamayori-hime|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q56344982}}, arrived at the seashore defying the wind and waves. As delivery neared, she entreated, “When I give birth, do not gaze into the delivery room.” Unable to contain his curiosity, the heavenly grandson secretly peered in. Transforming into a dragon, Toyotamahime, deeply ashamed of being spied upon, wrapped her newborn child in straw and abandoned it by the shore, then swiftly departed by sealing off the seacoast. The child came to be known as {{ill|Amatsu Hikohiko Nagakate Ukayafukiaezu|ja|彦波瀲武盧茲草葺不合尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amatsu Hikohiko Nagakate Ukayafukiaezu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. Some time later, Hikohodemi passed away, and it is said he was interred on a tumulus atop Takaya-yama in Himuka. ==== First Account (1) ==== The elder, {{ill|Hanoseri|ja|ホスセリ|lt=Hanoseri|lt_ja=火酢芹命|1=Hosuseri|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanoseri|13=User:Immanuelle/Hosuseri|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 火須勢理命}}, frequently obtained fortune from the sea, while the younger, Hikohodemi, often procured fortune from the mountains. At one time, the brothers agreed to exchange their fortunes. The elder ventured into the mountains with his brother’s bow but could not even find a trace of animal tracks; the younger, taking his brother’s fishing hook, went to the sea but caught no fish and lost the hook. When the elder returned the bow and demanded his original hook, the younger, in anguish, crafted a multitude of hooks from his side-sword and presented them in a basket, yet his brother angrily refused them, insisting on the original. Overwhelmed with sorrow, Hikohodemi wandered by the seashore until an old man appeared, calling himself Salt-and-Earth Old Man, and asked, “Who are you, and why do you suffer here?” After Hikohodemi explained, the old man took a black comb from his bag, tossed it onto the ground, and it transformed into a grove of 500 bamboo shoots. Gathering the bamboo, he constructed a large basket, placed Hikohodemi inside, and set him adrift into the sea. Alternatively, he fashioned a floating vessel from a bamboo basket and thin ropes, binding Hikohodemi to it before sending him off. Eventually, at the bottom of the sea a fine shore appeared naturally, and upon proceeding along it, Hikohodemi soon reached the palace of the sea god. There, the palace was as a castle—lofty and resplendent. Near a well outside the gate, beneath a Katsura tree, a beautiful maiden emerged from among her attendants to fetch water in a jewel-like vessel. Startled, she hurried back and told her divine parents, “There is a rare and noble guest beneath the tree by the well—truly of an uncommon appearance.” ==== First Account (2) ==== Hikohodemi, in his despair, wandered along a hundred-branch grove by a well; then an elderly man appeared, identified as Salt-and-Earth Old Man, and said, “Who are you, and why do you suffer?” After hearing his story, the old man produced a dark comb, threw it to the ground where it transformed into a grove of 500 bamboos, fashioned a large basket, and enclosed Hikohodemi within it before setting him adrift into the sea. (Or, alternatively, he made a floating vessel from a bamboo basket, bound him with thin ropes, and sent him off.) As the tide receded along the shore, the lost hook was recovered from the mouth of a fish, and the sea god called for it. He then returned the hook to Hikohodemi with instructions: when you return this hook to your brother, recite an incantation naming it “the root of poverty, the beginning of famine, the source of suffering.” Moreover, when you cross the sea, I will surely raise a tempest so that you shall not drown.[http://nihon.syoukoukai.com/modules/stories/index.php?lid=1470]{{ill|Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko|ja|海彦と山彦|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 山幸彦と海幸彦|1=Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11468336}} (Manga Japanese Folktales Database) ==== First Account (3) ==== The elder, {{ill|Hanoseri|ja|ホスセリ|lt=Hanoseri|lt_ja=火酢芹命|1=Hosuseri|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanoseri|13=User:Immanuelle/Hosuseri|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 火須勢理命}}, having acquired much from the sea, came to be called Umisachihiko, while the younger, Hikohodemi, who gained much from the mountains, was called Yamasachihiko. Although the elder repeatedly lost his tools to wind and rain, the younger never did. One day, the elder proposed an exchange of fortunes with his brother; the elder took the younger’s bow, venturing into the mountains to hunt, while the younger took the elder’s fishing hook to fish in the sea—yet neither secured any catch and returned empty-handed. When the elder, having reclaimed the bow, demanded his original hook, the younger, at a loss, fashioned a new hook from his side-sword and presented it en masse in a basket. Enraged, the elder declared, “I still desire my original hook!” In his despair, Hikohodemi could only lament. Later, while wandering and sighing bitterly by the sea, he encountered an elderly man who identified himself as Salt-and-Earth Old Man. After hearing his tale, the old man produced a mysterious object from a bag and, casting it to the ground, transformed it into a grove of bamboo. He then constructed a basket and placed Hikohodemi inside, setting him adrift. In time, Hikohodemi reached the palace of the sea god, where the deity, recognizing the divine virtue in the younger, eventually relented and made him his servant. It is said that the descendants of {{ill|Hanoseri|ja|ホスセリ|lt=Hanoseri|lt_ja=火酢芹命|1=Hosuseri|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanoseri|13=User:Immanuelle/Hosuseri|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 火須勢理命}}, the forebears of the Hayato, still remain near the palace walls as ever-vigilant watchdogs.{{Cite book |language=ja |title=隼人（古代の南部九州の居住民） |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E9%9A%BC%E4%BA%BA%28%E5%8F%A4%E4%BB%A3%E3%81%AE%E5%8D%97%E9%83%A8%E4%B9%9D%E5%B7%9E%E3%81%AE%E5%B1%85%E4%BD%8F%E6%B0%91%29-1578344 |publisher=[[:en:Kotobank|Kotobank]] |author1=Shōgakukan Nihon Daihyakusen (Nipponica) |authorlink1=小学館 }} ==== First Account (4) ==== Here, Hikohodemi came to be known as {{ill|Hoiorisuru|ja|火折尊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hoiorisuru|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ホオリ|1=Hoori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1051960}} until he encountered Salt-and-Earth Old Man; the narrative from Account (3) is similar. The old man then said, “Fret not; I shall now contrive a plan.” Measuring and declaring, “The excellent steed upon which the sea god rides is none other than an 1‐sun (approximately 30 cm) sea crocodile. Its back is erected at Tachibana’s small gate—indeed, let us devise a scheme with it.” Accompanied by Hoiorisuru, they set out to inspect. At that time, a sea crocodile announced, “After eight days, I shall deliver the heavenly grandson to the sea palace. However, my noble steed is but a 1‐sun crocodile. In a single day, it will surely be accomplished. Now, I must return to summon my lord; ride well and enter the sea. When you do so, a fine shore will naturally appear along the course, and if you proceed along it, you will undoubtedly reach my lord’s palace. At the palace gate, above the well, a Yutsukatsura tree shall be found—take your place there.” No sooner had he spoken than he plunged into the sea. Accordingly, the heavenly grandson waited as instructed; when eight days had passed, a 1‐sun sea crocodile arrived, and he boarded it to enter the sea—each act in accordance with the crocodile’s earlier counsel. Meanwhile, as Toyotamahime’s attendant, bearing a jewel-like bowl, attempted to draw water from the well and noticed a figure at the bottom, she could not manage to scoop the water and looked up at the heavenly grandson. Immediately, she returned to report to her lord, “Our lord appears uniquely resplendent—indeed, a solitary guest of surpassing excellence is present; he is far superior.” The sea god, upon hearing this, said, “I shall observe this.” He then prepared three mats and received the guest. There, the heavenly grandson sat with his feet on the edge of the mat, his hands pressed on the inner mat, and on a sumptuous futon he reclined. Recognizing him as the heavenly god’s grandson, the sea god’s veneration grew ever deeper. Later, when the sea god summoned the red-finned maiden ({{ill|Red Sea Bream|ja|赤鯛|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Red Sea Bream|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}/{{ill|Nayoshi|ja|鯔魚・なよし|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) and inquired, she produced the fishing hook from her mouth. At that moment, the sea god imparted it to Hikohodemi with the command: “When you return this hook to your brother, speak these words: ‘O great hook, the hook of poverty, of destitution, and of idiocy,’ and then, after finishing your speech, cast it aside.” He further instructed that when your brother ventures into the sea to fish, you should remain by the shore to raise a wind—namely, a gust that is a whistle. Thus, I will raise the western and border winds to send forth surging waves to overwhelm him.” Hoiorisuru then returned, having faithfully followed the sea god’s instructions. On the day the elder fished, the younger whistled by the shore; in an instant, a swift wind arose, and the elder, overwhelmed, began to drown with no hope of rescue. In desperation, he called out to his distant brother, “You have long tarried on the open sea; surely there must be a way—please, save me! If I survive, may I forever remain as your servant, or even be known as a ‘dog-man.’ I implore you.” Hearing this, the younger ceased his whistling, and the wind died away. The elder, realizing the divine virtue possessed by his brother, finally submitted. Thus, when the younger produced Shioyutsutama, the elder raised his hands and was engulfed by the tide; when Shiohifurutama was presented, he was restored. Prior to this, as they were parting, Toyotamahime had said, “I am already with child; very soon I shall deliver. Please build a delivery hut for me by the seashore.” Following her words, Toyotamahime later arrived and said to Hikohodemi, “Tonight, I intend to give birth. Do not come near.” Hikohodemi, however, disobeyed and lit a fire on a comb to peep in. In response, Toyotamahime transformed into a massive eight-span crocodile and crawled prostrate. Deeply shamed, she vowed never again to suffer such humiliation and, after wrapping her child in straw and placing it by the shore, departed into the sea. Alternatively, it is said that rather than abandoning her child on the shore, Toyotamahime herself carried the infant and left, later declaring that “It is not proper for the heavenly grandson’s child to be left in the sea,” and thus she entrusted her child to her younger sister, {{ill|Toyotamahime|ja|玉依姫|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyotamahime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タマヨリビメ|1=Tamayori-hime|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q56344982}}. Soon after, disturbed by the child’s handsome appearance, Toyotamahime’s compassion grew, and she wished to reclaim the child for rearing; but being unable to do so on principle, she sent her younger sister to care for him, along with a parting song. == Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko == The “Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko” myth has exerted a great influence on Japanese folktales and is transmitted throughout Japan in the form of “{{ill|Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko|ja|海彦と山彦|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 山幸彦と海幸彦|1=Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11468336}}.” == Influence on the Urashima Tarō Legend == This myth of “Umisachihiko and Yamasachihiko” is said to have served as a model for the various local legends of [[:en:Urashima Tarō|Urashima Tarō]] throughout Japan.[https://www.asukanet.gr.jp/tobira/urashima/urashima.html][[:en:Urashima Tarō|Urashima Tarō]] (Ancient History Portal) [[:en:Hoori|Hoori]]（{{ill|Hikohohodemi|ja|ヒコホホデミ|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hikohohodemi|1=Hikohohodemi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11329989}}）。]] '''Yamasachihiko to Umisachihiko''' (山幸彦と海幸彦) is, in the {{ill|Kiki|ja|記紀|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Kiki|WD=Q842308}}, a mythologized struggle between the {{ill|Tenson-zoku|fr|ja|天孫族|zh|天孫民族|en:draft|simple|User:Immanuelle/Tenson-zoku|ko|천손족|uk|Тенсон Зоку|lt=Tenson Tribe|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenson-zoku|qq=}} and the [[:en:Hayato people|Hayato Tribe]].[http://dictionary.goo.ne.jp/leaf/jn2/20434/m0u/]{{ill|Digital Daijisen|ja|デジタル大辞泉|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Digital Daijisen|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大辞泉|1=Daijisen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q5209153}} [[:en:Shogakukan|Shōgakukan]]（{{ill|Umisachi Yamasa|ja|海幸山幸|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Umisachi Yamasa|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 山幸彦と海幸彦|1=Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11468336}}） 2013-09-11 viewed{{Cite book |language=ja |title={{ill|Umisachi Yamasa|ja|海幸山幸|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Umisachi Yamasa|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 山幸彦と海幸彦|1=Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11468336}} |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%B5%B7%E5%B9%B8%E5%B1%B1%E5%B9%B8-441493#E5.A4.A7.E8.BE.9E.E6.9E.97.20.E7.AC.AC.E4.B8.89.E7.89.88 |publisher=[[:en:Kotobank|Kotobank]] |author1=Sanseidō Daijirin Third Edition |authorlink1=大辞林 }} . It is mainly known as “{{ill|Umisachi Yamasa|ja|海幸山幸|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Umisachi Yamasa|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 山幸彦と海幸彦|1=Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11468336}}” (うみさちやまさち). == Overview == Within the myth, the naming as recorded in the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]] is as follows: ;Kojiki Nomenclature :'''Yamasachihiko''' – [[:en:Hoori|Hikohodemi]] (in the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]]) and Hikohodemi (in the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]]) :'''Umisachihiko''' – [[:en:Hoderi|Hoteri]] (in the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]]) and KouRankou (in the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]]) As their names imply, the tale tells of the younger Yamasachihiko, skilled in mountain hunting ([[:en:Mountain|Mountain]]), and the elder Umisachihiko, adept at fishing in the sea ([[:en:Sea|Sea]]). The [[:en:Brother|Brothers]] at one time exchanged their implements: Yamasachihiko went fishing ([[:en:Angling|Fishing for Fish]]) but lost the borrowed {{ill|Fishing Hook|ja|釣針|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fishing Hook|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 釣り針|1=fishing hook|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q205276}}, while his elder brother could not procure his game with his own tools. In his distress, Yamasachihiko was instructed by {{ill|Shiotsuchi-no-Oji|lt=Shiotsuchi-no-Oji|lt=Shiotsuchi no Oji|ja|シオツチオジ|lt=Shiochitsu no Kami|lt_ja=塩椎神|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shiotsuchi no Oji|qq=}} (also read “しおつちのかみ”) to board a small boat and head for the {{ill|Watatsumi Shrine|ja|綿津見神宮|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Watatsumi Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (also understood as the Palace of the Sea God). Welcomed by the sea deity ([[:en:Watatsumi|Great Watatsumi]]), Yamasachihiko later married the daughter [[:en:Toyotama-hime|Toyotamahime]] (also known as Toyotamahime, i.e. {{ill|Toyotamahime|ja|豊玉毘売命|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyotamahime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to トヨタマヒメ|1=Toyotama-hime|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2329261}}) and enjoyed three blissful years at the Watatsumi Shrine. However, needing to return to the land, Yamasachihiko received from Toyotamahime the lost fishing hook along with two mystically endowed orbs, “Shioyutsutama” (潮盈珠) and “Shiohifurutama” (潮乾珠). Using these, he is said to have subdued Umisachihiko and compelled him to pledge loyalty. This Umisachihiko is also regarded as the progenitor of the trading [[:en:Hayato people|Hayato]] tribe. Subsequently, Toyotamahime bore a child – identified as [[:en:Ugayafukiaezu|Ugayafukiaezu]] (reading: うがやふきあえずのみこと) – and Yamasachihiko came to be recognized as the grandfather of [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]] (via his link to the [[:en:Grandparent|Grandfather]]). == Synopsis == === Kojiki === ==== Umisachibiko and Yamasachibiko ==== In the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]], {{ill|Hoteri|ja|火照命|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hoteri|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ホデリ|1=Hoderi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2716491}} (ほでりのみこと) is portrayed as Umisachibiko, a fisherman who caught fish of all sizes, while {{ill|Hikohodemi|ja|火遠理命|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hikohodemi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ホオリ|1=Hoori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1051960}} (ほおりのみこと) is depicted as Yamasachibiko, a hunter who captured beasts of every size. Hikohodemi proposed that the brothers exchange their tools; though Hoteri refused thrice, he eventually consented to a temporary swap. Using his brother’s fishing hook (referred to as “Umisachi”), Hikohodemi attempted to catch fish but failed utterly—and, to make matters worse, lost the hook in the sea. When Hoteri, unable to secure any catch with his own implements, demanded the return of his original tool with the remark, “Neither mountain nor sea yield their fortunes unless one uses one’s own implements,” he reproached his brother. In despair, Hikohodemi fashioned 1,000 hooks from his own {{ill|Ten Fist Sword|ja|十拳剣|1=Totsuka-no-Tsurugi|lt=Ten Fist Sword (alternate)|lt_ja=十拳劔|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ten Fist Sword|13=User:Immanuelle/Totsuka-no-Tsurugi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 十束剣}}, yet Hoteri insisted he desired only the original. ==== Watatsumi God's Palace ==== Hikohodemi then set out for the palace of the sea deity at the {{ill|Watatsumi Shrine|ja|綿津見神の宮殿|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Watatsumi Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (originally linked via the anchor in the “Ryūgū” article). While waiting there, a [[:en:Handmaiden|maidservant]] of the sea god’s daughter, [[:en:Toyotama-hime|Toyotamahime]], went out to draw water. When Hikohodemi requested water, the maidservant filled a vessel and presented it; however, instead of drinking, he placed an orb he wore about his neck into the vessel. The orb clung stubbornly to the vessel, prompting the maidservant to relay the incident to Toyotamahime. Startled by the sight of Hikohodemi, Toyotamahime fell in love at first sight. Her father, the sea god himself, emerged and declared that Hikohodemi was none other than the son of {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi|ja|邇々芸命|lt=Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi|lt_ja=邇々芸命|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninigi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (a descendant of the heavenly grandson revered by the fish for their pledged loyalty), and immediately arranged for their marriage. Thus, Hikohodemi lived for three years in the palace of the sea god. ==== Submission of Hoteri ==== After three years, recalling his original purpose for having come, Hoteri lamented deeply. When the sea god inquired about the cause of his sorrow, Hoteri explained. Gathering the fish, the sea god discovered that one red [[:en:Red seabream|Red Sea Bream]] had the lost hook snagged in its throat. He then presented Hoteri with the fishing hook along with the orbs “Shioyutsutama” and “Shiohifurutama,” instructing him: “Return this hook to your brother while uttering: ‘This hook, be it a hook of melancholy, disquiet, poverty, or foolishness,’ and then, if your brother builds a rice field on high ground, you must build yours on low ground; if he builds on low, you build on high. Should he attack, submerge him with Shioyutsutama; and if, in suffering, he begs forgiveness, rescue him with Shiohifurutama.” He then sent him off riding on {{ill|Wani (mythology)|ja|和邇 (神話)|lt=Wani|lt_ja=和邇|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wani (mythology)|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 和邇|1=wani|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q20049265}}, now identified as {{ill|Saimotonomi|ja|佐比持神|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saimotonomi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. Hoteri thus returned the hook as directed and cultivated his own fields accordingly. As the sea god controlled the waters, Hoteri’s fields were left parched, and he grew increasingly impoverished. Moreover, when Hoteri became wrathful and launched an attack, Hoteri used Shioyutsutama to submerge him; and when Hoteri, wracked with pain, repented, Shiohifurutama was used to rescue him. Repeating this cycle until his torment abated, Hoteri finally bowed his head and vowed to guard Hoteri day and night. ==== The Birth of Toyotamahime ==== After conceiving at the sea palace, Toyotamahime could not bear to deliver a child in the depths and ascended to the land. Intending to build a delivery hut by the seashore, she went into labor before the thatched roof (made of egret feathers) could be completed, and thus entered the delivery hut. She instructed Hikohodemi, “When a person of another land gives birth, they assume their true form. I too intend to deliver in my true form, so under no circumstances should you look inside.” However, curious, Hikohodemi peered inside the hut and witnessed Toyotamahime transformed into Yahiro Wani, with her belly undulating like a serpent. Horrified, he fled. Ashamed of having spied, Toyotamahime, in her distress, returned to the sea, leaving behind the newborn child, who came to be known as [[:en:Ugayafukiaezu|Amatsu Hikohiko Nagakate Ukayafukiaezu]]. Nonetheless, harboring resentment over his peering, Hoteri, in order to raise the child, sent his younger sister [[:en:Tamayori-hime (mother of Jimmu)|Toyotamahime]] along with a parting song exchanged between them. === Nihon Shoki, Section 10 === In the main text of volume 2 of the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]], it is said that the elder, Hoteri, naturally possessed a fishing hook (representing “Umisachi”), while the younger, Hikohodemi, naturally possessed a bow and arrow (representing “Yamasachi”). Initially, the two brothers conversed and decided to test their fortunes by an exchange; but neither managed to obtain any catch. The elder, in his remorse, returned his brother’s bow and demanded his own hook. The younger, having already lost the hook in the sea and unable to retrieve it, fashioned another from his side-sword, assembling a heap in a single basket, but his brother rejected it, insisting instead on the original hook. In despair, Hikohodemi wandered along the seashore, lamenting. There he encountered {{ill|Salt-and-Earth Old Man|ja|塩土老翁|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Salt-and-Earth Old Man|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to シオツチオジ|1=Shiotsuchi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11174872}}, who said, “Worry not; I shall devise a plan for you.” The old man constructed a basket and placed Hikohodemi inside before setting him adrift at sea. In time, he reached a fine shore; abandoning the basket, he proceeded and soon arrived at the sea god’s palace. There, the palace was arranged with the elegance of a princely abode. By a well at the gate grew a tree of {{ill|Yutsukatsura|ja|湯津杜|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yutsukatsura|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, its branches and leaves spreading wide. As Hikohodemi advanced beneath the tree in a state of aimless wandering, a beautiful maiden opened a door and stepped out to fetch water using a lovely bowl. When she saw him, she stared intently; startled, she hurried back and informed her parents, “There is a most rare guest beneath the tree by the well at the gate.” The sea god then spread out multiple layers of tatami mats to welcome him, seating him with courtesy and inquiring the reason for his arrival. Hikohodemi explained his circumstances. When the sea god gathered fish to question them, all answered, “We know not—only that a red-finned fish with a troubled mouth (possibly a red [[:en:Red seabream|Red Sea Bream]]) has appeared.” Upon inspecting the fish’s mouth, the lost hook was recovered. Thereafter, Hikohodemi married the sea god’s daughter, Toyotamahime, and dwelled in the sea palace for three years. Although life there was peaceful and joyful, his longing for his homeland would sometimes bring deep sighs. Hearing this, Toyotamahime said to her father, “Surely the heavenly grandson laments, for he must miss his native land.” The sea god then summoned Hikohodemi, presented him with the previously retrieved hook, and instructed: “When you return this hook to your brother, quietly call it ‘the hook of poverty, of misfortune, of despair, and of folly.’” He also bestowed upon him the orbs “Shioyutsutama” and “Shiohifurutama,” advising: “Dip the former and your brother will be overwhelmed by the tide; if he repents, dip the latter and he shall be restored. In this way, he will naturally submit.” When it came time to depart, Toyotamahime told the heavenly grandson, “I am with child; the time for delivery is near. Please, construct a delivery room for me by the seashore.” Hikohodemi then returned to his original palace and followed the sea god’s instructions. Meanwhile, Hoteri, beset by troubles, eventually submitted, proclaiming, “From now on, I shall be your servant. Please show me mercy.” Thus, in accordance with his request, he was spared—and Hoteri is said to be the ancestor of figures such as Atano-kimi and small bridge figures, among others. Later, as promised, Toyotamahime, accompanied by her younger sister {{ill|Toyotamahime|ja|玉依姫|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyotamahime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タマヨリビメ|1=Tamayori-hime|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q56344982}}, arrived at the seashore defying the wind and waves. As delivery neared, she entreated, “When I give birth, do not gaze into the delivery room.” Unable to contain his curiosity, the heavenly grandson secretly peered in. Transforming into a dragon, Toyotamahime, deeply ashamed of being spied upon, wrapped her newborn child in straw and abandoned it by the shore, then swiftly departed by sealing off the seacoast. The child came to be known as {{ill|Amatsu Hikohiko Nagakate Ukayafukiaezu|ja|彦波瀲武盧茲草葺不合尊|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amatsu Hikohiko Nagakate Ukayafukiaezu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. Some time later, Hikohodemi passed away, and it is said he was interred on a tumulus atop Takaya-yama in Himuka. ==== First Account (1) ==== The elder, {{ill|Hanoseri|ja|ホスセリ|lt=Hanoseri|lt_ja=火酢芹命|1=Hosuseri|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanoseri|13=User:Immanuelle/Hosuseri|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 火須勢理命}}, frequently obtained fortune from the sea, while the younger, Hikohodemi, often procured fortune from the mountains. At one time, the brothers agreed to exchange their fortunes. The elder ventured into the mountains with his brother’s bow but could not even find a trace of animal tracks; the younger, taking his brother’s fishing hook, went to the sea but caught no fish and lost the hook. When the elder returned the bow and demanded his original hook, the younger, in anguish, crafted a multitude of hooks from his side-sword and presented them in a basket, yet his brother angrily refused them, insisting on the original. Overwhelmed with sorrow, Hikohodemi wandered by the seashore until an old man appeared, calling himself Salt-and-Earth Old Man, and asked, “Who are you, and why do you suffer here?” After Hikohodemi explained, the old man took a black comb from his bag, tossed it onto the ground, and it transformed into a grove of 500 bamboo shoots. Gathering the bamboo, he constructed a large basket, placed Hikohodemi inside, and set him adrift into the sea. Alternatively, he fashioned a floating vessel from a bamboo basket and thin ropes, binding Hikohodemi to it before sending him off. Eventually, at the bottom of the sea a fine shore appeared naturally, and upon proceeding along it, Hikohodemi soon reached the palace of the sea god. There, the palace was as a castle—lofty and resplendent. Near a well outside the gate, beneath a Katsura tree, a beautiful maiden emerged from among her attendants to fetch water in a jewel-like vessel. Startled, she hurried back and told her divine parents, “There is a rare and noble guest beneath the tree by the well—truly of an uncommon appearance.” ==== First Account (2) ==== Hikohodemi, in his despair, wandered along a hundred-branch grove by a well; then an elderly man appeared, identified as Salt-and-Earth Old Man, and said, “Who are you, and why do you suffer?” After hearing his story, the old man produced a dark comb, threw it to the ground where it transformed into a grove of 500 bamboos, fashioned a large basket, and enclosed Hikohodemi within it before setting him adrift into the sea. (Or, alternatively, he made a floating vessel from a bamboo basket, bound him with thin ropes, and sent him off.) As the tide receded along the shore, the lost hook was recovered from the mouth of a fish, and the sea god called for it. He then returned the hook to Hikohodemi with instructions: when you return this hook to your brother, recite an incantation naming it “the root of poverty, the beginning of famine, the source of suffering.” Moreover, when you cross the sea, I will surely raise a tempest so that you shall not drown.[http://nihon.syoukoukai.com/modules/stories/index.php?lid=1470]{{ill|Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko|ja|海彦と山彦|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 山幸彦と海幸彦|1=Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11468336}} (Manga Japanese Folktales Database) ==== First Account (3) ==== The elder, {{ill|Hanoseri|ja|ホスセリ|lt=Hanoseri|lt_ja=火酢芹命|1=Hosuseri|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanoseri|13=User:Immanuelle/Hosuseri|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 火須勢理命}}, having acquired much from the sea, came to be called Umisachihiko, while the younger, Hikohodemi, who gained much from the mountains, was called Yamasachihiko. Although the elder repeatedly lost his tools to wind and rain, the younger never did. One day, the elder proposed an exchange of fortunes with his brother; the elder took the younger’s bow, venturing into the mountains to hunt, while the younger took the elder’s fishing hook to fish in the sea—yet neither secured any catch and returned empty-handed. When the elder, having reclaimed the bow, demanded his original hook, the younger, at a loss, fashioned a new hook from his side-sword and presented it en masse in a basket. Enraged, the elder declared, “I still desire my original hook!” In his despair, Hikohodemi could only lament. Later, while wandering and sighing bitterly by the sea, he encountered an elderly man who identified himself as Salt-and-Earth Old Man. After hearing his tale, the old man produced a mysterious object from a bag and, casting it to the ground, transformed it into a grove of bamboo. He then constructed a basket and placed Hikohodemi inside, setting him adrift. In time, Hikohodemi reached the palace of the sea god, where the deity, recognizing the divine virtue in the younger, eventually relented and made him his servant. It is said that the descendants of {{ill|Hanoseri|ja|ホスセリ|lt=Hanoseri|lt_ja=火酢芹命|1=Hosuseri|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanoseri|13=User:Immanuelle/Hosuseri|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 火須勢理命}}, the forebears of the Hayato, still remain near the palace walls as ever-vigilant watchdogs.{{Cite book |language=ja |title=隼人（古代の南部九州の居住民） |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E9%9A%BC%E4%BA%BA%28%E5%8F%A4%E4%BB%A3%E3%81%AE%E5%8D%97%E9%83%A8%E4%B9%9D%E5%B7%9E%E3%81%AE%E5%B1%85%E4%BD%8F%E6%B0%91%29-1578344 |publisher=[[:en:Kotobank|Kotobank]] |author1=Shōgakukan Nihon Daihyakusen (Nipponica) |authorlink1=小学館 }} ==== First Account (4) ==== Here, Hikohodemi came to be known as {{ill|Hoiorisuru|ja|火折尊|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hoiorisuru|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ホオリ|1=Hoori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1051960}} until he encountered Salt-and-Earth Old Man; the narrative from Account (3) is similar. The old man then said, “Fret not; I shall now contrive a plan.” Measuring and declaring, “The excellent steed upon which the sea god rides is none other than an 1‐sun (approximately 30 cm) sea crocodile. Its back is erected at Tachibana’s small gate—indeed, let us devise a scheme with it.” Accompanied by Hoiorisuru, they set out to inspect. At that time, a sea crocodile announced, “After eight days, I shall deliver the heavenly grandson to the sea palace. However, my noble steed is but a 1‐sun crocodile. In a single day, it will surely be accomplished. Now, I must return to summon my lord; ride well and enter the sea. When you do so, a fine shore will naturally appear along the course, and if you proceed along it, you will undoubtedly reach my lord’s palace. At the palace gate, above the well, a Yutsukatsura tree shall be found—take your place there.” No sooner had he spoken than he plunged into the sea. Accordingly, the heavenly grandson waited as instructed; when eight days had passed, a 1‐sun sea crocodile arrived, and he boarded it to enter the sea—each act in accordance with the crocodile’s earlier counsel. Meanwhile, as Toyotamahime’s attendant, bearing a jewel-like bowl, attempted to draw water from the well and noticed a figure at the bottom, she could not manage to scoop the water and looked up at the heavenly grandson. Immediately, she returned to report to her lord, “Our lord appears uniquely resplendent—indeed, a solitary guest of surpassing excellence is present; he is far superior.” The sea god, upon hearing this, said, “I shall observe this.” He then prepared three mats and received the guest. There, the heavenly grandson sat with his feet on the edge of the mat, his hands pressed on the inner mat, and on a sumptuous futon he reclined. Recognizing him as the heavenly god’s grandson, the sea god’s veneration grew ever deeper. Later, when the sea god summoned the red-finned maiden ({{ill|Red Sea Bream|ja|赤鯛|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Red Sea Bream|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}/{{ill|Nayoshi|ja|鯔魚・なよし|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) and inquired, she produced the fishing hook from her mouth. At that moment, the sea god imparted it to Hikohodemi with the command: “When you return this hook to your brother, speak these words: ‘O great hook, the hook of poverty, of destitution, and of idiocy,’ and then, after finishing your speech, cast it aside.” He further instructed that when your brother ventures into the sea to fish, you should remain by the shore to raise a wind—namely, a gust that is a whistle. Thus, I will raise the western and border winds to send forth surging waves to overwhelm him.” Hoiorisuru then returned, having faithfully followed the sea god’s instructions. On the day the elder fished, the younger whistled by the shore; in an instant, a swift wind arose, and the elder, overwhelmed, began to drown with no hope of rescue. In desperation, he called out to his distant brother, “You have long tarried on the open sea; surely there must be a way—please, save me! If I survive, may I forever remain as your servant, or even be known as a ‘dog-man.’ I implore you.” Hearing this, the younger ceased his whistling, and the wind died away. The elder, realizing the divine virtue possessed by his brother, finally submitted. Thus, when the younger produced Shioyutsutama, the elder raised his hands and was engulfed by the tide; when Shiohifurutama was presented, he was restored. Prior to this, as they were parting, Toyotamahime had said, “I am already with child; very soon I shall deliver. Please build a delivery hut for me by the seashore.” Following her words, Toyotamahime later arrived and said to Hikohodemi, “Tonight, I intend to give birth. Do not come near.” Hikohodemi, however, disobeyed and lit a fire on a comb to peep in. In response, Toyotamahime transformed into a massive eight-span crocodile and crawled prostrate. Deeply shamed, she vowed never again to suffer such humiliation and, after wrapping her child in straw and placing it by the shore, departed into the sea. Alternatively, it is said that rather than abandoning her child on the shore, Toyotamahime herself carried the infant and left, later declaring that “It is not proper for the heavenly grandson’s child to be left in the sea,” and thus she entrusted her child to her younger sister, {{ill|Toyotamahime|ja|玉依姫|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyotamahime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タマヨリビメ|1=Tamayori-hime|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q56344982}}. Soon after, disturbed by the child’s handsome appearance, Toyotamahime’s compassion grew, and she wished to reclaim the child for rearing; but being unable to do so on principle, she sent her younger sister to care for him, along with a parting song. == Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko == The “Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko” myth has exerted a great influence on Japanese folktales and is transmitted throughout Japan in the form of “{{ill|Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko|ja|海彦と山彦|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Umi Hiko and Yama Hiko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 山幸彦と海幸彦|1=Yamasachihiko and Umisachihiko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11468336}}.” == Influence on the Urashima Tarō Legend == This myth of “Umisachihiko and Yamasachihiko” is said to have served as a model for the various local legends of [[:en:Urashima Tarō|Urashima Tarō]] throughout Japan.[https://www.asukanet.gr.jp/tobira/urashima/urashima.html][[:en:Urashima Tarō|Urashima Tarō]] (Ancient History Portal)
